faq.a: Not meaningfully. Unlike LDL, Lp(a) is mostly genetic and changes little with diet or exercise.
No. It contains an LDL-like particle but has an extra protein that gives it different effects, and standard LDL tests do not measure it separately.
faq.q: Is Lp(a) the same as LDL?

name: Understanding Lp(a)
blurb: What Lp(a) is, why it is inherited and how it damages arteries and valves.
title: Understanding Lp(a)
answer: Lp(a) is an LDL-like particle with apolipoprotein(a) attached, made in the liver and set mostly by variation in the LPA gene. It promotes plaque, inflammation and clotting, and it is a recognised causal risk factor for heart disease and aortic stenosis.

sections.body: A high Lp(a) explains why some people have heart disease despite good LDL; it is a reason for closer attention, not a verdict.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
The particle has three parts that matter. Its LDL-like core carries cholesterol into artery walls like LDL does. Its apolipoprotein(a) chain resembles plasminogen, a protein that dissolves clots, and may interfere with clot breakdown. And Lp(a) carries oxidised phospholipids, molecules linked to inflammation in artery walls and valves.

Levels vary enormously between people, from almost none to many times average, mostly because of the LPA gene. The gene contains a variable number of repeated segments called kringle IV type 2 repeats; fewer repeats make a smaller apolipoprotein(a), which the liver releases more efficiently, giving higher levels. Levels also differ on average between ancestry groups, which is one reason a single risk cutoff fits poorly for everyone.

developments.text: A 2026 review describes Lp(a) as 70 to 90 percent heritable, largely unresponsive to lifestyle, and an independent causal risk factor for atherosclerotic disease and calcific aortic stenosis.
